title: Development and experimental implementation of noise characterisation techniques on a superconducting quantum processor
authors: Nelson M. M. Fernández, Francesco Grieco, Hetta Vappula, Stefano Mangini, Boris Sokolov, Elsi-Mari Borrelli, Matteo A. C. Rossi, Sergey N. Filippov, N. Walter Talarico
abstract: Noise characterisation not only enables error mitigation but also provides valuable information about the intrinsic performance of a quantum device, identifying dominant error contributions and bounding noise stability well beyond the aggregated calibration data. Deploying such methods on a specific hardware topology must combine efficiency and accuracy, assess noise stability, and validate the reconstructed noise model. Here we develop and implement these methods on a superconducting processor with square-lattice topology. First, we revise the cycle-benchmarking protocol and reduce the bias arising from unlearnable degrees of freedom via a regularised cost function. Second, we extend a previously developed tensor-network tomography method to match the device layout and show how its accuracy can be improved by repeated layer execution. Both methods allow approximate sublayer noise models to be extracted from parent ones. Using noise characterisation as a tool, we map the noise structure, track drift, and validate the adequacy of the learnt noise models against experimentally observed noisy estimations in benchmark physical and chemistry circuits. These results inform further improvements in the underlying technology and provide estimates of the size of noise-mitigated circuits that the device can support.
summary: This paper details the development and experimental implementation of advanced noise characterization techniques on a superconducting quantum processor. By revising benchmarking protocols and extending tensor-network tomography, the authors successfully map the noise structure and validate noise models against physical circuits. This research is crucial for understanding hardware limitations and estimating the reliable scale of quantum computation.
main_problem: The paper addresses the critical need to accurately characterize noise sources in superconducting quantum processors to enable robust error mitigation and estimate achievable circuit sizes.
main_result: The developed noise characterization techniques allow for the extraction and validation of approximate sublayer noise models, demonstrating that the total estimation error can be kept below 13% for moderately deep circuits.
method: The authors employ revised cycle-benchmarking protocols and extended tensor-network tomography methods to map the noise structure by measuring the decay of Pauli expectation values.
model_or_system: The work is performed on a superconducting quantum processor with a square-lattice topology (VTT Q50), utilizing transmon-based qubits and flux-tunable couplers.
key_observables: Pauli expectation values (decay curves), gate infidelities (PRX, CZ, RO), and the total estimation error in benchmark circuits.
important_parameters: Noise rates ($\lambda_k$), circuit depth (L=15), and width (N=50) for performance estimation.
main_assumptions: Key assumptions include treating single-qubit gate errors as negligible compared to two-qubit errors, and the noise channel acting before each layer of Clifford gates.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the coupling map and fidelities of the processor, the cumulative distribution of gate infidelities, and comparisons between measured signal decay and predictions from single-layer versus jointly fitted multi-layer noise models.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first introducing the necessity of noise characterization, detailing the revised cycle-benchmarking and tensor-network methods, and finally applying these tools to map the noise structure and validate the learned models against physical and chemical benchmark circuits.
why_interesting: This work provides concrete, hardware-specific methodologies for quantifying noise in superconducting qubits, which is foundational knowledge for any theoretical physicist working on open quantum systems or quantum computation.

Fi- nally, all qubits are measured.
